subject: chemistry
title: Carbon-carbon bond formation and nitriles
key_idea: Chain lengthening needs a new C–C bond. CN⁻ adds one carbon to a haloalkane or a carbonyl compound, and the nitrile can then be reduced to an amine or hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid.

blocks.text: Most reactions you have met change the functional group but keep the same carbon skeleton. To build a bigger molecule, a chemist must form a new carbon-carbon bond. This section covers why that matters and which reactions do it.

items: Chain lengthening adds one or more carbon atoms to a molecule.
It is how small, cheap starting materials become the larger molecules needed for medicines, plastics and dyes.
Few reagents do it, so each one is worth knowing.

items.meaning: A species that donates a lone pair of electrons to form a new bond.
A compound containing the –C≡N group. The carbon of the group is a new carbon added to the chain.
A compound with an –OH group and a –C≡N group on the same carbon.

items: A new C–C bond is needed whenever the carbon skeleton must grow.
Cyanide ions are the main nucleophile used to add one carbon.

blocks.text: Cyanide ion, CN⁻, is a good nucleophile and carries one carbon. There are two ways to use it, depending on the starting material.

items: Heat the haloalkane under reflux with **KCN** dissolved in **ethanol**.
Ethanol is used as the solvent. If water were present, the OH⁻ ion would compete and an alcohol would form.
The mechanism is nucleophilic substitution: CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon and the halide ion leaves.
Add **HCN** to the carbonyl compound, with KCN as a catalyst, and warm gently.
The mechanism is nucleophilic addition.
The product is a hydroxynitrile, one carbon longer.

items.text: CN⁻ uses its lone pair to attack the δ+ carbon of C=O.
The C=O π bond breaks and both electrons move onto oxygen, giving a negative intermediate.
The O⁻ takes H⁺ from HCN (or water), forming the hydroxynitrile and releasing CN⁻ to start again.

blocks.text: The C=O group is planar, so CN⁻ can attack from either face with equal chance. Most hydroxynitriles from aldehydes and unsymmetrical ketones form as a racemic mixture.
Hydrogen cyanide and cyanide salts are very toxic. Reactions are done in a fume cupboard, with the HCN made in the flask from the cyanide salt and acid.

items: Haloalkane + KCN in ethanol, heated, gives a nitrile by nucleophilic substitution.
Aldehyde or ketone + HCN with KCN catalyst gives a hydroxynitrile by nucleophilic addition.
Both add exactly one carbon.

blocks.text: A nitrile can be converted into two useful functional groups. This section covers reduction to an amine and hydrolysis to a carboxylic acid.

items: Hydrogen gas over a **nickel** catalyst reduces C≡N to a primary amine.
The product is a primary amine that is one CH₂ longer than the original haloalkane.
Heat the nitrile under reflux with **dilute acid**, such as dilute hydrochloric acid.
The product is a carboxylic acid, and the nitrogen leaves as an ammonium ion.
With dilute alkali, the product is a carboxylate salt and ammonia. Acidify afterwards to free the carboxylic acid.

blocks.label: Acid hydrolysis of a nitrile
where: Product: propanoic acid, plus ammonium ions

diagram.alt: Pick a reaction to see the reagents, the product and the change in chain length.

options.label: Bromoethane to a nitrile
results: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux

options.label: Ethanal to a hydroxynitrile
results: HCN with KCN catalyst, gentle warming

options.label: Propanenitrile to an amine
results: None. The nitrile carbon is already in the chain.

options.label: Propanenitrile to an acid
results: None. The nitrile carbon becomes the COOH carbon.

items: Reduction with H₂ and nickel turns a nitrile into a primary amine.
Hydrolysis with dilute acid turns a nitrile into a carboxylic acid.
Bromoethane to propanoic acid is a two-step route that adds one carbon.

checks.q: Give the reagent and conditions that turn 1-bromopropane into butanenitrile, and name the type of mechanism.
checks.a: KCN dissolved in ethanol; heat under reflux. Nucleophilic substitution.

checks.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of propanone with HCN and KCN catalyst.
checks.a: CN⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon of C=O; the C=O π electrons move to oxygen giving an O⁻ intermediate; O⁻ takes H⁺ from HCN (or water) to give 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile and regenerates CN⁻.

checks.q: Starting from bromoethane, give a two-step route to propanoic acid with reagents.
checks.a: Step 1: KCN in ethanol, heat, giving propanenitrile. Step 2: heat under reflux with dilute HCl (or dilute NaOH then acidify) to give propanoic acid.

blocks.text: A benzene ring can also be given a longer side chain. The Friedel–Crafts reaction forms a new C–C bond between the ring and a carbon chain.

items: **Alkylation**: benzene reacts with a haloalkane such as chloromethane, giving an alkylbenzene and HCl.
**Acylation**: benzene reacts with an acyl chloride such as ethanoyl chloride, giving a phenyl ketone and HCl.
Both need anhydrous conditions and a **halogen carrier** catalyst, such as AlCl₃ or FeCl₃.
The halogen carrier reacts with the haloalkane or acyl chloride to make a positive electrophile (R⁺ or RCO⁺) and AlCl₄⁻.
The electrophile substitutes for an H on the ring by electrophilic substitution.
The AlCl₄⁻ removes the H⁺, giving back AlCl₃ and forming HCl, so the catalyst is regenerated.

blocks.text: Grignard reagents are organomagnesium compounds that add carbon atoms through a new C–C bond. They are made in dry ether and used at once.

items: Make the reagent by adding **magnesium** to a haloalkane in **dry ether**, such as ethoxyethane.
The product, RMgBr, has a carbon with a partial negative charge, so it acts as a nucleophile.
Water must be absent. It would react with the Grignard reagent to give an alkane, RH.

blocks.label: Making a Grignard reagent
where: In dry ether, no water present

rows: A carboxylic acid, one carbon longer than the Grignard's R group

items: The Grignard's carbon attacks the δ+ carbon of C=O, adding the whole R group to that carbon.
A second step with dilute acid releases the alcohol or carboxylic acid from its magnesium salt.
